claim: APOBEC3G (A3G) is an enzyme expressed in primates with the potential to inhibit human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infectivity.
source: APOBEC3G (A3G), an enzyme expressed in primates with the potential to inhibit human immunodeﬁciency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infectivity, is a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) deoxycytidine deaminase with two domains, a catalytically active, weakly ssDNA binding C-terminal domain (CTD) and a catalytically inactive, strongly ssDNA binding N-terminal domain (NTD).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of A3G.

claim: A3G is a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) deoxycytidine deaminase.
source: APOBEC3G (A3G), an enzyme expressed in primates with the potential to inhibit human immunodeﬁciency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infectivity, is a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) deoxycytidine deaminase with two domains, a catalytically active, weakly ssDNA binding C-terminal domain (CTD) and a catalytically inactive, strongly ssDNA binding N-terminal domain (NTD).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of A3G.

claim: A3G has two domains: a catalytically active, weakly ssDNA binding C-terminal domain (CTD) and a catalytically inactive, strongly ssDNA binding N-terminal domain (NTD).
source: APOBEC3G (A3G), an enzyme expressed in primates with the potential to inhibit human immunodeﬁciency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infectivity, is a single-stranded DNA (ssDNA) deoxycytidine deaminase with two domains, a catalytically active, weakly ssDNA binding C-terminal domain (CTD) and a catalytically inactive, strongly ssDNA binding N-terminal domain (NTD).
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a defining characteristic of A3G.

claim: A3G binds ssDNA in multiple steps and in two distinct conformations, distinguished by degree of ssDNA contraction.
source: A3G binds ssDNA in multiple steps and in two distinct conformations, distinguished by degree of ssDNA contraction.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by optical tweezers measurements throughout the manuscript.

claim: A3G stabilizes formation of ssDNA loops.
source: A3G stabilizes formation of ssDNA loops, an ability inhibited by A3G oligomerization.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: A3G oligomerization inhibits the ability of A3G to stabilize ssDNA loops.
source: A3G stabilizes formation of ssDNA loops, an ability inhibited by A3G oligomerization.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data comparing WT and FW mutant A3G.

claim: A3G securely binds ssDNA through the NTD, while the CTD samples and potentially deaminates the substrate.
source: Our data suggests A3G securely binds ssDNA through the NTD, while the CTD samples and potentially deaminates the substrate.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Oligomerization of A3G stabilizes ssDNA binding but inhibits the CTD's search function.
source: Oligomerization of A3G stabilizes ssDNA binding but inhibits the CTD's search function.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data comparing WT and FW mutant A3G.

claim: A3G's binding mechanisms explain its ability to efficiently deaminate numerous sites across a 10,000 base viral genome during the reverse transcription process.
source: These processes explain A3G's ability to efficiently deaminate numerous sites across a 10,000 base viral genome during the reverse transcription process.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings and their implications for A3G function.

claim: A3G inhibits the infectivity of HIV-1 when it is not targeted for degradation by the accessory protein viral infectivity factor (Vif).
source: APOBEC3G (A3G) is particularly known for its ability to inhibit the infectivity of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) (Harris and Liddament, 2004; Malim, 2009) when it is not targeted for degradation by the accessory protein viral infectivity factor (Vif) (Desimmie et al., 2014; Fisher et al., 1987; Goila-Gaur and Strebel, 2008; Sheehy et al., 2002; Strebel et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G primarily functions as a cytidine deaminase, catalyzing the conversion of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine on single-stranded DNA.
source: A3G primarily functions as a cytidine deaminase (Suspène et al., 2004; Yu et al., 2004), catalyzing the conversion of deoxycytidine to deoxyuridine on single-stranded DNA (ssDNA).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G-mediated deamination can result in DNA degradation through cleavage due to the presence of U bases in the viral DNA or G to A base mutations in the complementary DNA, impairing viral replication.
source: A3G-mediated deamination can result in DNA degradation through cleavage due to the presence of U bases in the viral DNA or G to A base mutations in the complementary DNA, impairing viral replication (Lecossier et al., 2003; Mangeat et al., 2003; Pollpeter et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G consists of two zinc coordinating domains.
source: Structurally, A3G consists of two zinc coordinating domains.
evidence: This is stated as a structural characteristic of A3G.

claim: For two domain APOBEC3 proteins, only one domain is enzymatically active.
source: Other members of the APOBEC3 family also have either one or two domains, though for two domain proteins only one domain is enzymatically active (LaRue et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: For A3G, the C-terminal domain (CTD) is enzymatically active.
source: For A3G, the C-terminal domain (CTD) is enzymatically active (Haché et al., 2005; Navarro et al., 2005), though when isolated it binds ssDNA with low affinity (Chelico et al., 2010; Harjes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: When isolated, the A3G CTD binds ssDNA with low affinity.
source: For A3G, the C-terminal domain (CTD) is enzymatically active (Haché et al., 2005; Navarro et al., 2005), though when isolated it binds ssDNA with low affinity (Chelico et al., 2010; Harjes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The A3G N-terminal domain (NTD), though lacking deaminase activity, binds ssDNA and RNA with high affinity.
source: In contrast, the N-terminal domain (NTD), though lacking deaminase activity, binds ssDNA and RNA with high affinity (Chelico et al., 2010; Huthoff et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The NTD is critical in A3G's packaging in the virion.
source: The NTD is critical in A3G's packaging in the virion and also contains the binding site for Vif (Navarro et al., 2005; Russell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The NTD contains the binding site for Vif.
source: The NTD is critical in A3G's packaging in the virion and also contains the binding site for Vif (Navarro et al., 2005; Russell et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G has a self-affinity and oligomerizes, especially when bound to nucleic acids.
source: A3G also has a self-affinity and oligomerizes, especially when bound to nucleic acids (Chelico et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A3G oligomerization on ssDNA greatly slows dissociation.
source: A3G oligomerization on ssDNA greatly slows dissociation (Chaurasiya et al., 2014; Morse et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The NTD is important for A3G dimerization.
source: The NTD is important for A3G dimerization, and mutation of two aromatic residues within the NTD (F126/W127), causes A3G to remain monomeric, even when bound to ssDNA (Chelico et al., 2010; Morse et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Mutation of two aromatic residues within the NTD (F126/W127) causes A3G to remain monomeric, even when bound to ssDNA.
source: The NTD is important for A3G dimerization, and mutation of two aromatic residues within the NTD (F126/W127), causes A3G to remain monomeric, even when bound to ssDNA (Chelico et al., 2010; Morse et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G mutants lacking enzymatic function retain a significant degree of anti-viral function.
source: Despite the importance of A3G deamination activity, it has been shown that even A3G mutants lacking enzymatic function retain a significant degree of anti-viral function (Gillick et al., 2013; Iwatani et al., 2006; Luo et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2005), suggesting A3G also has a deamination-independent mode of suppressing HIV-1 infectivity (Holmes et al., 2007; Iwatani et al., 2007; Levin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G has a deamination-independent mode of suppressing HIV-1 infectivity.
source: Despite the importance of A3G deamination activity, it has been shown that even A3G mutants lacking enzymatic function retain a significant degree of anti-viral function (Gillick et al., 2013; Iwatani et al., 2006; Luo et al., 2007; Newman et al., 2005), suggesting A3G also has a deamination-independent mode of suppressing HIV-1 infectivity (Holmes et al., 2007; Iwatani et al., 2007; Levin et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: Only 7 ± 4 A3G monomers are packaged in the virion.
source: Even for WT A3G in the absence of Vif, only 7 ± 4 A3G monomers are packaged in the virion (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A3G uses facilitated diffusion to speed up the search for target deamination sites.
source: A3G has been shown to use facilitated diffusion to speed up the search for target deamination sites (Chelico et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A3G can slide along the negatively charged ssDNA strand in a 1-dimensional manner to travel short distances.
source: Positively charged A3G can slide along the negatively charged ssDNA strand in a 1-dimensional manner to travel short distances or move larger distances by either dissociating from the ssDNA, diffusing in 3-dimensions, and rebinding at a new random site, or by directly transferring from one part of the strand to another (Feng et al., 2014; Nowarski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G can move larger distances by dissociating from the ssDNA, diffusing in 3-dimensions, and rebinding at a new random site.
source: Positively charged A3G can slide along the negatively charged ssDNA strand in a 1-dimensional manner to travel short distances or move larger distances by either dissociating from the ssDNA, diffusing in 3-dimensions, and rebinding at a new random site, or by directly transferring from one part of the strand to another (Feng et al., 2014; Nowarski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: A3G can move larger distances by directly transferring from one part of the strand to another.
source: Positively charged A3G can slide along the negatively charged ssDNA strand in a 1-dimensional manner to travel short distances or move larger distances by either dissociating from the ssDNA, diffusing in 3-dimensions, and rebinding at a new random site, or by directly transferring from one part of the strand to another (Feng et al., 2014; Nowarski et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The probability that A3G will deaminate a second neighboring site before dissociating is defined as enzyme processivity.
source: The probability that A3G will deaminate a second neighboring site before dissociating is defined as enzyme processivity and varies as a function of the distance between the two target sites and the presence of short segments of dsDNA or RNA/DNA hybrids (Ara et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a definition supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A3G processivity varies as a function of the distance between the two target sites and the presence of short segments of dsDNA or RNA/DNA hybrids.
source: The probability that A3G will deaminate a second neighboring site before dissociating is defined as enzyme processivity and varies as a function of the distance between the two target sites and the presence of short segments of dsDNA or RNA/DNA hybrids (Ara et al., 2014).

claim: The inability of A3G to deaminate sites close to the 3′ end of a ssDNA substrate suggests that the catalytically active binding state for A3G positions the CTD towards the 5′ end.
source: The inability of A3G to deaminate sites close to the 3′ end of a ssDNA substrate suggests that the catalytically active binding state for A3G positions the CTD towards the 5′ end, such that the inactive NTD occupies this 'dead zone' (Chelico et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A3G moves bidirectionally along ssDNA.
source: Additionally, although A3G moves bidirectionally along ssDNA, as it lacks an energy source for directed motion and instead relies on thermally driven diffusion (Senavirathne et al., 2012), the enzyme acts processively only while deaminating in the 3′ to 5′ direction along the ssDNA substrate (Chelico et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: A3G lacks an energy source for directed motion and instead relies on thermally driven diffusion.

source: AFM studies have also directly observed the binding and oligomerization of A3G to ssDNA under a variety of conditions, including the observation that A3G is able to form tetramers on a 69 nt long segment of ssDNA (Pan et al., 2018; Shlyakhtenko et al., 2011; Shlyakhtenko et al., 2012; Shlyakhtenko et al., 2013).

evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature and demonstrated in Figure 1A.

source: Fitting the FJC model to multiple ssDNA molecules returns average parameters of L = 0.565 ± 0.003 nm, p = 0.717 ± 0.024 nm, and S = 804 ± 36 pN (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), consistent with previous measurements under similar conditions (Smith et al., 1996).

source: A similar doubling of ssDNA persistence length has been previously observed for the binding of the single domain APOBEC3H (A3H) (Feng et al., 2018).

claim: The ssDNA aggregation is not the result of A3G oligomerization, but an activity of the monomer itself.

claim: The amplitude of the extension change is 10 times larger for the 2x ssDNA template as compared to the 1x ssDNA at 80 pN.

claim: The ssDNA-A3G system is well represented as a simple two state model in which A3G is bound to ssDNA in either a non-compacting or compacting conformation.
source: While it is possible the conformation and effective length of the ssDNA-A3G complex changes continuously as applied force deforms the complex, we find that this system is well represented as a simple two state model in which A3G is bound to ssDNA in either a non-compacting or compacting conformation (Figure 4A).

claim: At high forces, ssDNA loops are destabilized, and an overall increase in ssDNA extension is observed.

claim: When the force is decreased to 20 pN or less, the extension of the ssDNA decreases over time, consistent with bound A3G transitioning to the more compacting state.
source: The opposite effect is seen when the A3G is first equilibrated at 80 pN, free protein removed, and then the force decreased to 20 pN or less. The extension of the ssDNA decreases over time, consistent with bound A3G transitioning to the more compacting state.
evidence: This is an observation from the experimental data.

source: This 'V' shaped force dependence is characteristic of a two-state system, in which applied force decreases and increases the rate A3G assuming its compacting and non-compacting states, respectively.
